events.title: The row over Rutland: can England’s smallest county survive?
events.summary: Its council is due to merge with Leicestershire’s in 2028, and some locals are incensed. Can the county hold on to its ceremonial status – and biggest selling point? M ysterious disappearances have been taking place lately in Rutland, an East Midlands pocket between Leicestershire, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire that is often considered to be England’s smallest county . Usually, there are road signs when driving into a new county welcoming you over the border. But in recent months, these have been going missing. After 10 signs vanished, the council decided to remove the remaining 17. Now there are no official “Rutland” signs at all. The area’s MP, the Conservative Alicia Kearns, is “not sure” what the motivation behind the thefts is. But they are certainly a fitting metaphor for Rutland’s disappearing status: its council is due to merge with Leicestershire county council in spring 2028. The changes are part of the government’s plans to create 15 new councils across England , replacing smaller district and county councils with larger, single unitary authorities that would run services. The government says it is aiming to cut duplication in the older two-tier system and allow the new larger councils to focus on government priorities such as housebuilding. The new authorities will have a population of about 500,000 people; Rutland’s estimated population is just over 41,000. For the people of Rutland, this marks nothing short of “having our identity stripped from us”, according to a statement on Kearns’s website . It’s sparked a campaign to Save Rutland. A petition presented to parliament earlier in the year was signed in person by 7,141 people. In an age of Change.org petitions circulated on social media, it feels oddly quaint to hear of a paper and pen petition. But that is Rutland in a nutshell, I realise shortly after stepping off the train in its county town of Oakham: oddly quaint. At Oakham Castle, there are more than 200 horseshoes on display , a result of the “horseshoe toll” that any visiting member of the royal family or peer of the realm must, to this day, pay (the most recent horseshoe payment was made in 2024 when the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh visited). As I spend the day travelling around the county (conveniently, no journey takes more than 15 minutes by car), everyone I meet is quick to extol its community spirit, its safety, its beauty – something I can see for myself as I pass clusters of thatched cottages surrounded by fields of sheep, and cutesy town centres where fences are lined with bunting. “The joke goes: ‘Rutland is England 50 years ago,’” says Kearns when we meet at the county’s most famous landmark, the UK’s largest reservoir by surface area, Rutland Water, home to the Rutland Osprey Project . She tells me about the county’s farming community, its tradition of Friday shoots that supply the local pubs with game, its pride in local businesses. So resistant are Rutlanders to some aspects of modernity, “we were the last county to have a McDonald’s built”, she says. Even when it did finally arrive , in 2020, the decision “was really controversial”. Kearns grew up in Cambridgeshire (although her mother’s family are from Rutland), moving to the county only after she was elected MP for Rutland and Stamford in 2019. But she has clearly fallen in love with the place she now calls home, and is passionate about protecting Rutland’s identity as a small, quirky, historic county. “Oakham Castle is the oldest English court building still in continuous use,” is just one of the Rutland facts she reels off in the car as we drive around. The county is also home to the National Leg Wrestling Championships and the World Nurdling Championship, she tells me, which involves players throwing pennies into a hole drilled into a wooden seat (“the winner’s called the best tosser”). A 10-metre-long “sea dragon” fossil was found in the county in 2022 . “What else? The first person to translate the Qur’an from Arabic into Latin came from Ketton,” which is another village in Rutland. To add to its quintessentially British charm, Rutland is full of excellent pubs. I visit one, the George & Dragon, in a village called Seaton. It’s everything you want a village pub to be, a small, stone-built country inn with mismatched chairs and wooden beams across the ceiling, buzzing with customers even at 5pm. I meet Ralph Offer, the owner, who, conversely, isn’t your stereotypical pub landlord – he is just 30 years old, having taken a loan out to buy the pub when he was 21. Clearly someone with a laser eye for business, he explains that the chance to visit the smallest county in England is Rutland’s “biggest selling point”, and helps to bring people to his pub, which also has rooms.

events.title: Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes
events.summary: Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions? It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon. One analysis written by Hamid Paktinat, the founder of the Forum of Economic Activists, suggests the construction of alternative pipelines and export routes by Iran’s Gulf neighbours will halve the strait’s strategic value within three years. Those who worry about wasting assets inevitably set store by the separate visits this week to Tehran of Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, and Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir. These two men are critical to renegotiating the terms for the reopening of the strait and the revival of the discarded memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June. The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have both recently made unusually blunt comments about the need to end the war – and the economic consequence of continuing it. Ghalibaf said that regardless of how much military power Iran possessed, “if people are hungry” and there was no economic growth, the country could not endure. Security, he argued, could not be sustained without a functioning economy. He added that, as someone with a military background, “we know the value of peace better than those who talk about peace”. Pezeshkian was even more blunt: “The war must end at some point,” he said. His argument was that Iran should end the conflict now, while Tehran still believes it is negotiating from a position of strength, rather than wait until its position weakens. The Iranian central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, also recently went on TV to warn about the economic pressures. “We are facing four or five major challenges simultaneously, including maximum sanctions, blockade, cutting off oil exports, and a budget imbalance, each of which puts pressure on the economy,” he said. “One of the neighbouring countries told me that if one-fifth of what happened in your country happened in our country, we would not be able to govern the country.” What is driving these remarks is the pressure on ordinary people in Iran, and an acceptance that the strait cannot become a permanent security doctrine in itself. Hamid Asefi, a Tehran-based journalist specialising in geo-economics, is one of many warning that if Hormuz is to be played as Iran’s final card every time a crisis arises, this card will gradually lose its value. “A threat that is constantly repeated turns from ‘deterrence’ into a political habit; and a political habit, if not accompanied by concrete achievements, sooner or later leads to an inflation of threats,” he said. The main question is no longer: can Iran close the strait, he wrote, but if Iran closes Hormuz to the world, does it open the door to power for itself or lock part of its power behind that door? “This is the Hormuz paradox. In international politics, a lever that is constantly flaunted can become its own enemy because it forces others to plan to reduce their vulnerability […] the main question of Iranian policy in Hormuz must change from: ‘How can we make the passage difficult?’ to ‘How can we make the passage so safe and stable that everyone needs Iran to maintain this order?’” That does not imply the lever is valueless. Far from it. According to data compiled by the ship tracker Kpler, only 112 oil and gas tankers went through the strait between 1 and 19 August. Almost 79% used unconfirmed routes, 19% used Iran’s preferred northern route and 2% used the Omani route. In reality many of the ships that used the unknown routes probably turned off their transponders and used US protection along the Oman route. It also appears that aided by the US government, Saudi, Emirati, Qatari and Kuwaiti oil companies have chartered a small group of oil tankers to take cargo through the southern route to the Gulf of Oman, where they then offload the oil to waiting tankers owned by their customers. Much of the risk is therefore transferred from shipping companies and oil customers to the more highly motivated state oil producers and to the US government. Iran has drawn up a blacklist of about 48 ships that it will try to ban or fine. But the US government is probably exaggerating the impact of these workarounds.

events.title: 'Unfortunate kick in the guts' as inflation data increases RBA rate hike risk
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Inflation slows again in July but heightens risk of interest rate hike by RBA Inflation eased again in July but some economists believe it has heightened the risk of an interest rate hike. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica ) Headline inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in the year to July, making it lower than before the Iran War in February. However, the RBA's preferred measure of inflation did not budge, staying at 3.6 per cent for the third straight month. Economists say the figures have increased the risk of a rate hike by the RBA at its September meeting. Economists have warned that another interest rate hike by Australia's central bank is a "live" possibility this year, despite inflation cooling again. Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the annual headline inflation rate rose to 3.5 per cent last month, down from 3.8 per cent for the year to June. Housing was the largest contributor to the Consumer Price Index in July, which increased by 5 per cent due to rising costs associated with new dwellings. Food inflation also increased by 3.2 per cent in the year to July, driven mostly by higher prices for dining out and takeaway meals, while annual inflation for transport rose 1.6 per cent. "On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 7.5 per cent in July after falling for three months in a row," said the ABS's head of price statistics Rachel McCririck. Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly. The headline rate of 3.5 per cent in July was slightly higher than the 3.3 per cent figure predicted by many economists, but the annual rate is now lower than it was before the start of the Iran war in February. Treasurer Jim Chalmers welcomed the "moderation" in annual inflation, but said he expected the data to fluctuate further in the coming months. "It does mean that inflation is substantially lower than the budget forecast, but we're under no illusions because we know that people are still under pressure," he said. "Fuel was a big driver of inflation in July and the fuel excise relief comes off in August, so we expect that to play out in next month's figures. "Inflation will bounce around a bit as it gets further down to the Reserve Bank's target range." The federal government's temporary fuel excise cut ended at the start of this month. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) The underlying inflation or "trimmed mean" figure preferred by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which strips out volatile items like fuel, remained unchanged at 3.6 per cent. The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. But the monthly trimmed mean figure increased to 0.5 per cent, leading economists to warn the figures could warrant a further interest rate hike from the RBA. "If you annualise that number, we get 3.6 [to] 3.8 per cent, so that's just way too far from the RBA's target [between 2.5 to 3 per cent]," said AMP economist My Bui. "And even on the annual numbers, it has been 3.6 per cent three months in a row, contrary to people's hope that it has been softening somewhat. Prior to the release of the July inflation data almost 83 per cent of economists polled by Reuters expected the RBA to keep interest rates on hold at its next meeting in late September. But Ms Bui said it was likely the RBA would be concerned by the figures and would consider lifting rates at a future meeting. "I think the RBA would be quite worried. Yesterday we got the minutes from their latest meeting and they actually admitted to us that they think the risk to inflation is on the upside," she said. "They should be quite worried … because the ABS said a lot of the drivers of inflation were concentrated in the sticky services area. The RBA considered raising interest rates at its meeting this month but elected to hold them at 4.35 per cent. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) David Bassanese, the chief economist at Betashares, said the figures meant the RBA's September meeting was "live". "Today's higher-than-expected underlying inflation result is an unfortunate kick in the guts for an already ailing economy as it increases the risk of yet another Reserve Bank interest rate increase at next month's policy meeting," he said. "The only question now is whether today's result is bad enough to force the RBA's hand as early as next month, or whether it would be prepared to wait for the following monthly inflation report on 30 September — which would be one day after its September policy meeting. "At this stage I still anticipate the RBA will hold fire.

events.title: Why Tesla has been caught up in a massive car recall in China
events.summary: Hidden door handles were popularised by Tesla Hidden car door handles - the sleek designs often found on electric vehicles (EVs) - have come under the spotlight over the past week. That's after China announced its biggest ever recall of cars, with more than four million vehicles - mostly Teslas - affected . The recall comes ahead of new regulations in China , requiring cars to have a mechanical release both on the inside and outside of their doors. Popularised by Elon Musk's electric vehicle giant, this type of handle has become commonplace around the world. But several incidents have raised concerns that this design may make doors difficult to open in an emergency. Hidden door handles are widely used in modern cars in China, with around 60% of the top 100 best-selling new energy vehicles, including EVs and hybrids, having them. The minimalist design gives vehicles a "sleek look and reduces wind drag" but can be confusing to use, car industry analyst Stephen Dyer from consultancy AlixPartners told the BBC. "Even I often find it difficult to locate the switch to open the door from the inside of an unfamiliar vehicle," said Dyer, who is based in Shanghai. But beyond their usability, the handles have been blamed for endangering the lives of drivers and passengers. Electronically powered door handles became an industry trend, but raised "real safety concerns" when doors failed to open promptly, delaying rescue efforts after accidents, said Nanyang Technological University associate professor Lyu Chen. "A door handle may seem simple, but it becomes safety-critical in the seconds after a crash," Chen said. Chinese carmaker Xiaomi faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2025 involving its SU7 model, when suspected electrical failures allegedly trapped occupants. One of the incidents took place on a highway in Tongling city, eastern China, killing three people, according to regional news coverage cited by state-controlled media Global Times. Relatives of the victims said the passengers were stuck in the car as the vehicle's doors could not be unlocked after the collision, the outlet said. The SU7 was Xiaomi's first electric vehicle At the time, Xiaomi's representatives said the SU7 had mechanical emergency release handles that function even without power, which are located at the bottom of each door. The company added at the time that it was investigating the matter and cooperating with the police. The latest models of the SU7 come with new door handles that can be opened without power. Xiaomi has not responded to BBC requests for comment. Tesla has also faced lawsuits in the US over its door handle designs. The company has been sued by the only survivor of a crash in 2024 involving a Cybertruck - Tesla's electric pickup - that killed three college students in California. Survivor Jordan Miller alleged that the Cybertruck's design trapped passengers in the burning vehicle and blocked their rescue. The car did not have door handles and the electronic buttons meant to open the doors failed to work, according to his lawyers from The Veen Firm. "When you design a vehicle with no mechanical way to open the doors from the outside, you are betting the electronics will work in every scenario, including a high-speed crash followed by a fire," said one of the lawyers in a statement. In court filings, Tesla denied any wrongdoing and said the Cybertruck is compliant with US federal safety standards, the Guardian reported. There have been other cases in the US of passengers, including children, allegedly being trapped in Tesla cars after the doors suddenly stopped working. The BBC has contacted Tesla for comment. What is being done about hidden handles? In February, China said it would ban hidden door handles, making it the first country to do so. The new rules, which take effect on 1 January 2027, mean new car designs without physical release mechanisms on the inside and outside of their doors cannot be sold. The cars' interior must also carry signs to show how to open the door. The measures in China come ahead of the US and European Union, which typically lead regulations around road safety and emissions, Dyer noted. One reason is likely to be the sheer number of EVs in China, he added. On 21 August, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced that Tesla and some major Chinese car makers - including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely - would recall more than four million vehicles. China will ban hidden door handles on cars sold in the country from next year The manufacturers were ordered to add warning labels inside vehicle doors to show passengers how to open them. Some cars will also get a software update that will lower their windows in the event of a crash. Tesla, which started selling the Model S sedan with hidden door handles in China in 2014, is recalling nearly three million cars, according to the SAMR.

events.title: India’s Ringg gets backing from Peak XV as it pushes voice AI past the phone call
events.summary: 🚨 Flash Sale 🚨 Get $100 off your Disrupt 2026 ticket Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt More than 76% of consumers in India prefer talking to businesses over a phone call, according to a recent study from Truecaller. Since voice is still consumers’ preferred way to communicate, that leaves a big opportunity to automate support and outreach calls using voice AI in the country. Voice AI startup Ringg, which already processes 20 million call attempts a month, is betting that volume keeps climbing over the coming months, and it just raised more money on that belief. The company said today it has landed $10 million from Peak XV Partners as an extension of its Series A. It had previously raised $5.5 million in a Series A round earlier this year, bringing the round’s total to $15.5 million. Ringg started life as a text-to-speech startup called DesiVocal, but training its own speech models proved expensive, so the founders moved up the stack — building voice AI agents for enterprises instead. Indian fintech Cred became its first customer, and Ringg has since signed Indian startups like Flipkart, Practo, Groww, and Policybazaar. “At the start, we were doing high-volume, low-complexity use cases like outbound calling, lead qualification, loan collection, and more. We quickly realized these are not sticky use cases, and so it’s always going to be a price game,” the startup’s co-founder Siddharth Tripathi told TechCrunch. Ringg still serves some of those simpler use cases, but it has set its sights on more complex workflows: appointment booking for healthcare clinics, abandoned-cart recovery for e-commerce sites, and onboarding/KYC (“know your customer”) checks for fintech apps. Tripathi said Ringg’s voice agent now runs across 1,200 clinics for the healthcare app Practo, helping patients book visits or follow up on next steps post-visit. Voice calls still make up over 70% of Ringg’s business, but the startup has started branching into other channels, including chat and WhatsApp. For some clients like Shell, it’s also automating browser-based support requests. “We are trying to position ourselves as a platform for agents that bring outcomes or get things done rather than voice agents for enterprises,” Tripathi said. Most of Ringg’s customers are based in India, with a handful in the Middle East and the U.S. But the startup isn’t trying to sell directly to U.S. companies; instead, it wants to partner with global capability centers in India — the offshore hubs multinationals increasingly lean on for back-office and support work — to sell automation capacity alongside human support. Tripathi said the company builds its own speech recognition and generation models and would eventually like to own the full voice stack, including infrastructure and deployment. For now, though, that remains too costly, so the product works as an orchestration layer, routing tasks to different models depending on the use case. Rishen Kapoor, a principal at Peak XV, said that because Ringg started as a research lab building its own models, that technical depth shows up in the complex use cases it’s now tackling. “Because of the technical capabilities, they can actually do these hard-won enterprise workflows end to end. They can complete these higher-value tasks like merchant onboarding, like L1 and L2 support, with quality and with consistency,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Voice AI in India is a crowded field. Model makers, including Deepgram , ElevenLabs , Cartesia , and local players like Sarvam and Smallest.ai , are all jockeying for pole position. Orchestration-focused startups like Bolna and Blue Machines are chasing the same layer Ringg occupies, while sector-focused players like Gnani and Arrowhead concentrate heavily on finance. That layered stack — model makers, orchestrators, and application-layer players all trying to lock in enterprise workflows — is itself the story. The money and the defensibility increasingly sit with whoever owns the customer relationship and the outcome. Ringg currently has 40 employees, with more than 15 hired in the last three months. The startup is hiring for forward-deployed engineer roles that combine technical chops with product management skills, along with researchers focused on bringing down the cost of running its models. events.title: Graham wins South Carolina Senate primary, vindicating Trump
events.summary: The News South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s primary for a full term, riding President Donald Trump’s endorsement to a narrow victory after a quick special election. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” Graham said of Trump at her victory party in Columbia. She immediately pivoted to the general election against Democrat Annie Andrews, warning that she advocates “turning confused little boys into little girls and vice versa.” Graham, who’d never sought office before being appointed to replace her brother Lindsey in the Senate, was backed by most of the state’s GOP leadership, and her allies — including MAGA Inc., the president’s super PAC — outspent her primary competitor, Rep. Ralph Norman. “We had $8 million spent against us,” Norman told his supporters, bemoaning the president’s decision to endorse Graham. “His policies are good. I never understood why he got in this race. It is what it is.” Graham built an insurmountable lead in the 7th Congressional District in and around Myrtle Beach, where Rep. Russell Fry endorsed her after losing his own Senate bid, and where the president flew in for a weekend rally. Norman carried his district and the upstate, where the Grahams were raised and where conservative voters had been most critical of the late senator. In the rest of the state, Graham prevailed — including in the Charleston area, where former governor and congressman Mark Sanford endorsed Norman after his own Senate campaign faltered. She linked herself directly to the president, telling voters that, unlike her brother, she’d get rid of the filibuster to pass Trump’s voter ID law, and said she’d never support amnesty for undocumented immigrants. The president was on the verge of getting another endorsee over the line in Oklahoma, where former state Sen. Mike Mazzei beat Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the runoff for the GOP nomination for governor. Mazzei did best with votes cast on Election Day, after Drummond had criticized the president’s plan to import beef to ameliorate the effects of his tariffs. “When he gets it wrong, I will speak up,” Drummond said of Trump. David’s view Graham’s campaign, powered by her brother’s old political operation, impressed Republicans. Graham’s candidacy sometimes didn’t. After last week’s only runoff debate, where the senator punted a question on Taiwan and explained that “foreign policy” wasn’t her expertise, Republicans upped their expectations for Norman, a House Freedom Caucus member who ran to Graham’s right. But she won, and the president got to claim another victory, which she was happy to attribute to him. His intervention in Oklahoma was just as impressive: Mazzei, whose top issue is ending the state income tax, didn’t have a political legacy to run on like Graham’s. Notable Ben Jacobs covered the final days of the South Carolina runoff for Slate, including the in-person Myrtle Beach rally that the president attended: “It’s never an ideal sign when a candidate’s support at an election-eve rally is less than unanimous.”

events.title: 'Cheap and attractive' lights sold online fail Australian compliance tests
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lighting bought through online sales platforms fails safety standards and poses fire and shock risks, experts warn Testing of more than 100 lighting products available through online marketplaces has alarmed the lighting industry. ( Supplied: Lighting Council of Australia ) The Lighting Council of Australia has released the results of testing of 131 lighting products available at popular online marketplaces. The report found almost three in four products failed to meet Australian standards and three products that underwent laboratory testing failed safety tests. The council has called for online retailers to pull non-compliant products from Australian websites. Experts have warned that people buying lighting products on online marketplaces may be putting themselves at serious risk, after a report found almost three in four products failed to meet Australian standards. The Lighting Council of Australia (LCA) assessed 131 lighting products purchased through popular websites including Temu, AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and Kogan. It found 73 per cent were non-compliant with Australian standards. Three downlights selected from the online marketplaces underwent independent laboratory testing. All three downlights failed a required safety test and caught fire when exposed to heat and flame. A surface-mounted LED ceiling light after undergoing testing. ( Supplied: Lighting Council of Australia ) Two of the samples were destroyed during a high-voltage strength test. The report noted two of the products that failed the laboratory testing are unable to be identified, traced or recalled because they did not carry a model number. "Even armed with laboratory evidence of serious safety defects, a regulator would struggle to identify the responsible supplier, compel a recall, or prevent the same product being re-listed the following day under a different seller name," the report said. "These are the two ways electrical products kill people: fire and shock," LCA chief executive Malcolm Richards said. "This is no longer a question of whether someone gets hurt. It is a question of when, and of who will be held responsible when it happens, and right now the answer to that is nobody." Mr Richards said the products are available at a "very cheap and attractive" price. "Home owners buy them thinking they're upgrading their lighting but all they're going to do is ignite a significant fire or cause a shock to someone in their own home." Malcolm Richards said he was "horrified" by the laboratory test results. ( ABC News: Tobi Loftus ) The report found Temu and AliExpress scored the worst, with none of the lighting products sampled from the platforms passing compliance. Only 8 per cent of tested Amazon lighting products passed, along with 12 per cent of eBay lighting products. Mr Richards said the council wrote to the platforms in June with the results. He said Temu was the only platform to remove all of its 240V lighting products from its Australian website, while Amazon, AliExpress and Kogan did not respond. Temu removed all of its 240V lighting products from its Australian website after the LCA wrote to the company. ( AP: Florence Lo ) "Temu proved this is fixable in a week," said Mr Richards. "The others had the same evidence for two months and are still selling. That is a choice, not a technical problem." Daniella Jacobs-Herd's mother is furious Temu has been approved for a government "safety pledge" while denying liability for her daughter's life-changing injuries. The council has called for the online marketplaces to pull all unregistered 240V lighting products from their Australian listings. It has also called for more regulatory powers and more legal accountability for online marketplaces selling electrical products. Bea Sherwood, senior campaigns and policy advisor at consumer advocacy group Choice, said research showed about 6 per cent of people buying products on online marketplaces suffered an injury or property damage due to an unsafe product. "We're not seeing isolated reports or incidents, we're seeing people who have experienced harm multiple times from buying products online," Ms Sherwood said. She said Australia's product safety regime was "a bit of a patchwork system". "I think a lot of people assume that products being sold online have to be safe before they're sold online and instore, but that's actually not the case" she said. Choice had similar experiences to the LCA when trying to raise concerns with the platforms, and Ms Sherwood said the online marketplaces had proved they were unwilling to remove dangerous products.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Land court rules minister can strip Brampton Enterprises of leases as resort falls into disrepair Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry The abandoned pool on Brampton Island. ( Supplied: Sailinguncut ) The Queensland Land Court has ruled that an island resort owner can be stripped of its leases after it failed to use the land for tourism and allowed it to fall into disrepair. Natural Resources Minister Dale Last told the court Brampton Enterprises did not adhere to its lease conditions. Brampton Enterprises has lodged an appeal against the decision, but no date for the appeal hearing has been set. An Australian company will appeal a Queensland Land Court decision, which will allow it to be stripped of its leases for an "abandoned" island resort. A ruling last week found two leases on Brampton Island, 35 kilometres north-east of Mackay, could be forfeited back to the state for a "breach of the lease conditions". Natural Resources Minister Dale Last will make a final decision on whether the land is retaken. The 14-hectare island resort was purchased in 2010 by Brampton Enterprises, a company linked to United Petroleum, and was closed a year later. Brampton Island in the Whitsundays was once a popular tourist destination. ( Supplied: Mackay Isaac Tourism ) Despite plans to build new facilities, the Land Court found the resort was "dilapidated to the point of falling down", and the tidal rock pool was being "reclaimed by the sea". The North Queensland island once hosted up to 220 guests at a time, included a three-hole golf course and had an operating airstrip. The abandoned Brampton Island resort is in ruins. ( Supplied: Twoflower Travels ) An inspection of Brampton Island ordered by Mr Last in December 2025, and referenced in the Land Court, found damage to buildings had been "accelerated" by tropical conditions. "Following the resort's reported closure in 2011, it appears likely that the assets have essentially been abandoned and left to be taken over by the ravages of nature," the inspection report said. Mr Last told the court in Mackay that the conditions of the lease had required Brampton Enterprises to use the land for tourism, and that the company's planning processes for a new resort did not fulfil the purpose of the land. Island developers request extension A company comes under fire after asking for more time to rebuild a resort on Brampton Island that suffered cyclone damage in 2011. Brampton Enterprises had argued the condition had only excluded them from using the land for non-tourism purposes and did not require active use. However, the Land Court said the conditions had been clear, and there was a direct obligation to use the land for actual tourism. It found it had been "too long" for planning and approval processes to be counted as required use, due to 15 years passing since the resort's closure. It also ruled the company had breached repair conditions, with buildings not maintained. The decaying swimming pool on Brampton Island. ( Supplied: Twoflower Travels ) The court also found Brampton Enterprises did not provide enough evidence it had kept invasive Singapore daisies under control on the island. The company told the court it "vigorously" opposed the forfeiture of the leases. A Department of Justice spokesperson said Brampton Enterprises lodged an appeal on August 24. No date or location has been set for an appeal hearing. Plans to build villas accommodating 30 guests on Brampton Island were approved by the Mackay Regional Council in 2015. The approval was extended on three occasions, including a five-year extension from July 2025. A bird's-eye view of the 2015 plans for the site. ( Supplied: Mackay Regional Council ) Plans were approved in 2015. ( Supplied: Mackay Regional Council ) Mackay resident Michelle Cox, 67, said the original resort was an important part of the community when she was a teenager. "We lived out at the mining towns, but whenever we came into Mackay itself, which was once a month, we would generally do a day trip over to Brampton Island," she said. "The resort was great. The food was basic, but we thought it was very good back then, and they often had live music playing. "I've been there recently when we took our own boat out to go fishing, and it was just sad to have a look down and see what it had become." Brampton Enterprises has been contacted for comment.

events.title: Trump's Saudi nuclear deal reaches Congress as experts warn of proliferation risk
events.summary: Trump has submitted a proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia on civil nuclear energy to Congress on Monday, according to an administration official. The accord will only move forward if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords, the official said. Experts have criticized the pact for not including a permanent prohibition on enrichment or reprocessing. President Donald Trump submitted a proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia on civil nuclear energy to Congress on Monday, starting a mandatory review period for a pact that would open the kingdom to U.S. nuclear technology. A U.S. official confirmed the submission to MS NOW, saying the agreement, led by the Department of Energy, is consistent with the Atomic Energy Act. The president's position remains unchanged: the accord will move forward only if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords, the official said. The Wall Street Journal reported the submission on Tuesday. The deal, reached in July , would allow U.S. companies to export civilian nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia. The 30-year accord also calls for the kingdom to build AP1000 reactors, a project worth tens of billions of dollars that would benefit Westinghouse, jointly owned by Canada-based Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management . Congress now has 90 days of continuous session to review the agreement, which would go into effect absent objection. U.S. cooperation with foreign nations to develop civilian nuclear power requires such review under the Atomic Energy Act. Trump has suggested the agreement's terms would prevent Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium. "There will be no enrichment of material!" the president said in a social media post last month, adding that the agreement is "totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords." Some Democratic lawmakers and nonproliferation advocates have criticized the pact for not including a permanent prohibition on enrichment or reprocessing, and for weakening standard controls against converting the technology to military use. Instead, the deal proposes a U.S.-built and operated enrichment facility subject to a two-year feasibility study . "Washington is right to strengthen its relationship with Riyadh, but it should not do so at the expense of its effective nuclear weapons nonproliferation standards," Matthew Kroenig, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank the Atlantic Council, said in July . Kroenig expects the two-year feasibility study to conclude that Saudi Arabia should rely solely on imported fuel-cycle services, as most countries with peaceful nuclear programs do. "This would be a much better outcome than exporting a bomb-making capability to an additional country in an already volatile region," he said. The landmark agreement also comes at a time when the decades-long U.S.-led global nuclear order is already fraying , said Erin Dumbacher, Stanton nuclear security senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. "It takes a distinct approach from the stringent nonproliferation measures the United States has insisted on in the past when exporting nuclear energy," said Dumbacher, who also served in the Department of Defense in the Office of the Under Secretary for Policy. "It becomes a slippery slope toward more countries having nuclear material without the measures that have kept the total number of countries with nuclear weapons to only nine. More nuclear material unchecked around the world could lead to accidents, security risks, and more proliferation," said Dumbacher. Riyadh has indicated that it would not normalize ties with Israel unless an independent Palestinian state is recognized, a position that has hardened since the Gaza war began in 2023. Saudi officials have also said the kingdom would pursue nuclear weapons capability if Iran develops it.

events.title: Hungary files a criminal complaint over $965M COVID-19 ventilator deal, citing possible fraud
events.summary: Hungary's foreign ministry has filed a criminal complaint over possible fraud related to the previous government's purchase of ventilators during the COVID-19 pandemic BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungary's foreign ministry has filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors over what it says was possible fraud related to the previous government's purchase of ventilators worth some $965 million during the COVID-19 pandemic, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Tuesday. Hungary's previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán purchased the roughly 17,000 ventilators from China in March and April 2020, drawing criticism at the time that it was buying far more units than could be realistically deployed and paying much more per unit than other European countries. In a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Orbán, who is not related to the former prime minister, said the results of a ministry investigation into the purchase “raises suspicions of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly substantial financial loss and other criminal offenses.” She didn't detail specific allegations, but noted that the investigation involved tens of thousands of documents — some of which had to be recovered using digital tools “after unsuccessful attempts to delete them” — and raised further questions “about the responsibility of the ministry’s former senior leadership.” A statement released on the Hungarian government’s website on Tuesday pointed to other suspected irregularities related to the ventilator procurement, including that most of the units were purchased through intermediary companies that saw their revenues rise exponentially due to the transaction. Hungary's former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó cultivated close ties with China during his nearly 12 years in office, and oversaw the purchase of the ventilators as well as the procurement of 5 million doses of the China-produced Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine. Last month, Szijjártó resigned his seat in Parliament to take an executive position with Chinese automaker BYD, prompting accusations of a conflict of interest due to his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies given to the company while in office. events.title: From military alliance to economic partnership: How Trump is redefining U.S.-South Korea ties
events.summary: Alliance is pivoting from security to economics, as Trump scales back joint military exercises, according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Reduced exercises partly stem from Korea’s slow deployment of $350 billion investment commitments, compared to Japan: Politico. Downsizing U.S. military presence in Asia is a “fiasco” that could make countries pursue nuclear weapons: Richard Haass, Council on Foreign Relations. President Donald Trump 's move last week to scale back annual military drills with South Korea came as Seoul finalizes hundreds of billions of dollars in investment commitments to Washington. Trump's frustration over U.S. military spending overseas and stalled implementation of Korea's investments signal a shift in the allies' relationship from one based on security to economics, experts said. Doubts now remain about whether investments will ensure U.S. commitments to Korea's security, as many in Seoul and Washington hoped, said Darcie Draudt‑Véjares,​ a​ fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. She was referring to the $350 billion Korea promised to invest in the U.S. in exchange for lower "reciprocal" tariffs last year. "Looked at a different way, we could see a shift from a relationship centered around a military alliance to one centered around integrated industrial ecosystems," Draudt‑Véjares said. That puts "economics rather than security as the basis of the U.S.-South Korea partnership." Trump on Aug. 16 said that he had instructed the Pentagon to cut military drills because they were "costly" and send "inappropriate and hostile" signals to North Korea. The post was made around the time Korean Trade Minister Kim Jung-kwan arrived in Washington, D.C., to discuss the investment commitments and tariffs with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The order partly stemmed from Korea's slow pace of deploying the investments, compared to Japan, Politico reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Trump had canceled the annual exercises in 2018 as well after his historic meeting with Kim Jong Un in Singapore. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which traces its roots to 1954, involved around 18,000 Korean troops and an undisclosed number of American soldiers this year. U.S. Commerce Department and the Korean Trade Ministry did not respond to CNBC's requests for comments. It would be a mistake for allies to think that increased defense spending or economic ties will buy U.S. military commitment, said Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities. Semiconductor trade or cooperation on shipbuilding can continue, separate from the U.S. military presence in Asia, she said. "The terms of exchange might change, but a smaller military footprint and narrower set of commitments in Asia would also free U.S. economic resources for investment at home and abroad," she said. The two economies have deepened ties, particularly as Korean chip giants have become central to the global AI boom, with Nvidia as their most important client. Korean businesses are benefiting from Trump's push for reindustrialization aimed at getting ahead in the competition with China. Korean companies, for their part, have significantly increased investments across semiconductors, electric vehicles, and shipbuilding in the U.S. For example, Korean chip giant SK Hynix is building a $4 billion advanced packaging plant in Indiana and allocating $10 billion to invest in new product lines and back its U.S. business. But not all experts are convinced that scaling back the U.S. military footprint in Asia serves American interests. Trump's decision to cut the annual drills "further exacerbates allies' concerns of the unreliability of the U.S. as a security and economic partner," said Bruce Klingner, a former senior Central Intelligence Agency officer in the Koreas. He added that Trump is seeking to direct American voters' attention away from the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections in November. The shortened military exercises do not seem to have mollified North Korea. It launched more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea Thursday, the South Korean Defense Ministry said. Richard Haass, president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, said on "Squawk Box" last week that Trump's decision weakens the U.S.' credibility and leverage concerning North Korea. The greater danger is that South Korea could pursue nuclear weapons to protect itself, and it would be "incomparably worse because it would ultimately bring in China and potentially Japan," he said. "It's a fiasco."

events.title: Why rising heat is Asia’s next major health challenge
events.summary: Higher temperatures are putting new pressure on health systems across the region, prompting a broader push for awareness, prevention and earlier action Across the globe – and Asia in particular – the link between a changing climate and human health is becoming harder to ignore. Home to an estimated 60 per cent of the world’s population, Asia is warming faster than the global average and ranks among the planet’s most climate-disaster-prone regions. Yet public awareness has not kept pace with the scale of the threat. In Hong Kong, many residents remain unaware of the health risks posed by rising temperatures; they are also unaware of how simple behavioural changes could help reduce their exposure. Densely populated cities face particular risks. Concrete-heavy urban environments can trap heat, while air pollution, changing disease patterns and extreme weather events add to the burden. In 2024, Hong Kong recorded its hottest year on record, with 52 “very hot days” and 50 “hot nights”. This month, the city witnessed its hottest day on record. The “Climate and Health in Asia” report, produced by Forum for the Future and sponsored by AIA, describes extreme heat as a growing threat to population health. The risks are particularly acute in cities, where polluted air and the urban heat-island effect can compound exposure and keep temperatures elevated after sunset, prolonging exposure and endangering those most at risk. Asia’s rapidly ageing population must also be considered. By 2050, one in four people in the region are expected to be over 60, according to the report, increasing healthcare demand just as climate-related risks accelerate. “Human health is strongly determined by environmental health,” says Emily Chan, assistant dean and professor of Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Faculty of Medicine. “With climate change, there is a direct, visible and palpable impact on the population in Hong Kong. Research here shows that temperature extremes, sudden changes and especially summer heat have specific effects on mortality and morbidity across a range of diseases, as well as on the ability of the health system to cope.” Hot nights intensify the problem. “Research in Hong Kong found that a 24-hour cycle gives the community a chance to recover if nights are cooler than the daytime,” Chan says. “When the evening cooling period is shortened or disappears during periods of extreme heat, the risk multiplies for the general population, especially for vulnerable groups.” For Amita Chaudhury, AIA’s group head of sustainability and chair of the United Nations Principles for Sustainable Insurance Board, one of the biggest challenges is that climate-related health risks continue to be seen in isolation. “Climate change is still largely viewed as an environmental issue, yet factors such as extreme heat, poor air quality and severe weather are increasingly affecting the health and well-being of communities,” she says. “Many people see it as an inconvenience rather than a health risk, yet prolonged exposure can affect cardiovascular health, respiratory conditions, mental well-being and overall quality of life – particularly among older adults and those with pre-existing health conditions.” Globally, heat-related mortality among people over 65 has risen sharply compared with the 1990s, according to evidence cited in the report. For ageing societies such as Hong Kong’s, the trend highlights the need to treat extreme heat as something that is more than a seasonal inconvenience. “Research on temperature and health already shows that beyond certain thresholds, hospital admissions and deaths increase, depending on the disease,” Chan says. “If we consider the increasing number of hot days in the city over the past five years, there is good reason to believe that silent mortality and health service demand are increasing as well.” Heat is often described as a “silent disaster” – unlike a typhoon, heat does not always produce a clear moment of impact or trigger an equally visible community response. Yet the effects can accumulate across homes, workplaces, schools and hospitals. Chan says Hong Kong has the building blocks required for a stronger response, including reliable health data, skilled healthcare workers and the capacity to cope with emergencies. The challenge is ensuring these resources can be mobilised in real time when temperatures reach dangerous levels. The climate-health challenge also creates an opportunity to strengthen preparedness before illness occurs. Historically, healthcare protection has focused largely on treatment and recovery. Chaudhury says there is now a need to place greater emphasis on awareness, prevention and engagement to help people build resilience before health issues arise. AIA’s programmes reflect this broader shift towards prevention and long-term well-being.

events.title: Deloitte to pay $21.5 million to settle Trump administration's DEI investigation
events.summary: J. David Ake/Getty Images Deloitte agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle allegations related to Trump's crackdown on DEI. The DOJ accused Deloitte of discriminating on the basis of race and sex in its hiring practices. Deloitte did not admit liability in the settlement. Deloitte just became the latest company to face the consequences of President Donald Trump's crackdown on DEI, or diversity, equity, and inclusion practices. The Big Four professional services firm agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle allegations that it violated rules against employment discrimination in its federal contracts, the Department of Justice announced Tuesday. The agency accused Deloitte of discriminating on the basis of race and sex in its hiring and promotion practices. Deloitte did not admit liability as part of the settlement. The company said in a statement it was "pleased to have resolved this matter to avoid the cost and distraction of protracted litigation." The Justice Department called out DEI practices in its statement announcing the settlement. "Government contractors cannot reward or penalize employees based on race or sex — and labeling the practice DEI does not make it lawful," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "The Justice Department will aggressively pursue government contractors that have used taxpayer dollars to fund unlawful discrimination." The settlement is part of the Trump administration's broader probe of DEI practices at major companies with federal contracts. Several companies have pulled back on their DEI practices in recent years following pressure from conservatives and Trump's return to office. In early 2025, Deloitte cut some of its DEI policies and told some staff to remove their pronouns from their email signatures. In April, IBM agreed to pay $17 million to settle similar allegations of employment discrimination. IBM did not admit liability as part of the settlement. In a separate settlement also announced Tuesday by the state of Indiana, Deloitte agreed to pay $1.2 million over allegations that it violated nondiscrimination requirements in its work with the state. Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita's office said in a statement that the settlement was "the first of its kind between a state and a government contractor." events.title: Musk's rocket firm SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility
events.summary: Musk's SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility in Louisiana SpaceX already has facilities in Texas and Florida Published 26 August 2026, 01:39 BST Multi-billionaire Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX has announced that it will build its largest launch site yet in the southern US state of Louisiana. Construction of the $100bn (£73bn) project - named Starbase, Louisiana - is due to start next year, with the 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site expanding on the company's operations beyond its current Texas headquarters and locations in Florida. It will be used to "support thousands of Starship flights a year with missions launching to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond," SpaceX said on Tuesday. In June, SpaceX shares started trading on New York's technology-focused Nasdaq in the world's biggest ever stock market debut . SpaceX said it aims to launch its first Starship flight from the new Louisiana base in 2029. The facility will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region, the company said , external . The Louisiana Economic Development agency said the average wage of workers at the base - the largest of its kind in the world - would be 192% more than the region's current average salary. It will also create more than 8,100 new jobs indirectly, the agency estimated. "The historic project will establish Louisiana as a global hub for next-generation aerospace, with the capacity and infrastructure needed to dramatically increase launch frequency and expand access to space," it added. The facility in Louisiana will share its name with another SpaceX site on the southern tip of Texas. In 2025, residents in an area of Cameron County, where the company has testing and development operations, approved incorporating the patch of land as a city called Starbase . Inside the rural Texas town where Elon Musk is basing his business empire Published 20 April 2025 The SpaceX IPO made history. One month on has it lost momentum? Published 13 July Musk has set out ambitious goals for SpaceX, including plans to reach Mars, develop artificial intelligence (AI) models and launch data centres into space. In August, SpaceX and Tesla - Musk's electric vehicle and robotics firm - announced plans to build a $16.8bn artificial intelligence (AI) chip making complex in Texas called the Terafab. The facility aims to meet the companies' growing demand for computing power to support its projects including developing AI and robotics technology over the coming years. The newly-listed SpaceX is under pressure to convince investors that it will be profitable even as it pursues its expansion plans. Its shares have tumbled by more than 30% from the highs reached shortly after it began trading but are still higher than their $135 offer price. events.title: Court ruling threatens Republicans' midterm TV ad advantage
events.summary: A federal appeals court ruling Tuesday could erase a new midterm advantage for Republicans. Why it matters: The 2-1 ruling would block Republicans from using cash-rich party committees to buy more political TV ads at discounted rates. Republicans plan to appeal the decision, setting up another high-stakes campaign finance fight as the fall ad wars heat up ahead of November. Driving the news: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled the FCC was wrong to extend discounted candidate broadcast rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees that include non-candidate groups for ads they coordinate with candidates. The rates paid by super PACs and other outside groups are often several times higher than candidate rates. The case was brought by four Democratic candidates running this cycle — Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), former Gov. Roy Cooper (N.C.) and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (Mich.) The U.S. Supreme Court in June struck down limits on how much committees can spend in coordination with campaigns. Between the lines: Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance extending candidate rates to certain coordinated ads, would allow party committee cash to stretch further. The ruling applied to both parties. But while Democratic candidates generally have stronger grassroots fundraising, Republican Party committees have amassed larger war chests, fueled by megadonors Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance, allowed party committee cash to stretch further by accessing lower rates reserved for candidates. What they're saying: "Put plainly, today's ruling makes clear that lowest unit rate is an exclusive right given to candidates and incumbent campaigns and that is the law of the land," DSCC executive director Devan Barber and DCCC executive director Julie Merz said in a joint statement. "Democratic candidates' strong grassroots fundraising amplifying the voice of everyday Americans remains a fundamental advantage in the midterms," they continued. "This was an incorrect ruling that ignores decades of precedent," NRSC communications director Joanna Rodriguez said in a statement. "We plan on appealing and this is the first word not the last," she continued.

events.title: Sen. Darline Graham, Trump's pick for South Carolina Senate, wins GOP primary
events.summary: President Donald Trump threw his full-throated support behind Sen. Darline Graham to win the South Carolina GOP Senate nomination, despite questions about her fitness for the role. Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in a special primary runoff on Tuesday. Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, now advances to the general election against Democrat Annie Andrews in a safe Republican seat. Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster in July to finish the remainder of her brother's term, after he died unexpectedly at age 71. South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham staved off a challenge from Rep. Ralph Norman in the state's Senate primary runoff election, and with the help of President Donald Trump 's endorsement will advance to November's general election. Graham — the sister of Sen. Lindsey Graham, whose seat she was appointed to fill after he died unexpectedly in July — was leading Norman by 4 percentage points when the Associated Press called the race. She'll face Democrat Annie Andrews in November's general election. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter labels the race "Solid R." Lindsey Graham was favored to win reelection before his death. The race was a test of Trump's power of the party, as he threw his full support behind Graham. Trump, the de facto head of the party, has traditionally played kingmaker, but has suffered a series of recent losses. Graham and Norman are both Trump allies. But Norman, a hard-line member of the House Freedom Caucus, found himself crosswise with Trump on occasion, in part owing to his initial support for former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in the 2024 GOP presidential primaries. Norman also has a tendency to raise fiscal concerns about some of the president's priorities, at times straining his relationship with the president. Trump throughout this election cycle has targeted fellow Republican lawmakers who have opposed him or his policies. Graham , who has a brief political track record, has enjoyed Trump's enthusiastic support since the days after her brother's unexpected death.. Trump, who had a close relationship with Lindsey Graham, traveled to South Carolina to campaign with Graham last week and held a tele-rally for her on Monday. ″[T]here is nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life, and has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina," Trump posted to TruthSocial on Monday. Graham, who has never been elected to office but was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster in July to serve out the remainder of her brother's term, came into Tuesday on somewhat shaky ground. She suffered an embarrassing moment in a debate with Norman last week. Canada unveils retaliatory tariffs on about $20B of U.S. goods Trump targets Iran's trade lifelines — here are the countries most exposed Mark Walter's TWG Global hires Goldman vet Markowitz as top lawyer amid probe Trump oil and gas stocks gained up to $15.5 million, Democrats say Trump admin unveils anti-Iran global sanctions plan, signals China not exempt Asked to comment on the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests, Graham copped that she was "not that informed on national security," raising questions about her fitness for the job. Graham has since defended her performance, arguing during an appearance on Fox News that she doesn't "speak politician." Norman, who launched an unsuccessful bid for South Carolina governor earlier this year, seized on the moment, casting himself as the proven conservative in the race. "My opponent is unknown. She's being backed by the Washington establishment," Norman said in a recent appearance on Fox News . "She's a propped-up candidate. You could tell that during the debates. This is an important job. There is no training on the job that you can effectively do." The stakes were high for Trump, some of whose picks in South Carolina, as well as other parts of the country, have fallen short of late. Trump in May endorsed South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette in the GOP primary for governor, though he eventually co-endorsed state Attorney General Alan Wilson , who bested Evette in a runoff in June. GOP lawmakers in the South Carolina legislature also dealt a blow to Trump in May when they scuttled his push for partisan mid-decade redistricting. Elsewhere, too, Trump's once-powerful endorsement has come up short. Rep. Randy Feenstra , R-Iowa, in June lost to Zach Lahn in the state's GOP gubernatorial primary, despite notching support from Trump. A Trump-endorsed candidate lost this month in Wyoming's Republican gubernatorial primary . And two candidates Trump had backed for the House in Florida — Rep. Cory Mills and Catalina Lauf — lost their respective primaries earlier this month.

events.title: Adam Mosseri said Instagram struggled for years to get teens to use 'Take a Break'
events.summary: Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, testified that the app struggled for years to get teens to use its Take a Break well-being feature. Bloomberg/Getty Images Mosseri said Instagram struggled for years to get teens to use its Take a Break well-being feature. Instagram touted a 90% retention rate for Take a Break but omitted its 1.8% activation rate. Meta faces a high-stakes trial in Oakland over whether its platforms cause harm to teens. The head of Instagram said the company spent years trying to persuade teens to " take a break ." Adam Mosseri testified Tuesday on the witness stand in Meta's social media addiction trial in Oakland that relatively few teens initially opted into "Take a Break," a well-being feature designed to encourage users to step away from the app after a set amount of scrolling. "Most people don't turn it on, but I don't think we knew that yet because this was still under development," Mosseri told the jury. "Actually, we found out that a lot of people didn't turn it on, and we've had to make a lot of changes over the last few years in order to have it be more adopted. This was back in 2021." Mosseri said Instagram first tried showing teens notifications encouraging them to activate the reminders. The strategy produced some improvement, he said, but fell well short of the company's expectations. "It started very low. We started trying to do those notifications, encouraging teens to turn it on themselves," Mosseri said. "That helped, but not nearly as much as we had hoped. And then we eventually made it on by default as part of Teen Accounts ." A coalition of attorneys general, led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, has accused Meta of exploiting young users for profit by designing its platforms to keep them hooked. The states also allege that Meta violated children's privacy protections and misled the public about the platforms' safety. Tuesday's testimony also called into question how Instagram publicly presented Take a Break's performance. An internal Meta document shown during the testimony said adoption had been "modest at 1.8%" back in 2021. According to Instagram's public blog post in December 2021, 90% of teens who turned on Take a Break kept it on, which did not include the statistic that only 1.8% had activated the feature in the first place. "Early test results show that once teens set the reminders, more than 90% of them keep them on," Instagram wrote at the time. When asked whether the public post disclosed that adoption was low, Mosseri said, "No, because we were planning on iterating on it and trying to drive that number up over time, which we did." "My expectation is that we were going to raise awareness and let the teens who want the feature turn it on," Mosseri said. "Turned out most teens didn't want it. We decided to push forward with it anyway." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP Senate runoff
events.summary: Sen. Darline Graham , President Trump's endorsed candidate, won the Republican nomination Tuesday to fill the Senate vacancy created by her brother Lindsey Graham 's death, per the AP. Why it matters: The victory underscores Trump's continued sway with Republican voters and positions Graham as the odds-on favorite to win a full term in November. Graham, 62, will be heavily favored against Democrat Annie Andrews in November . Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in South Carolina since 1998. Driving the news : Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman finished first and second , respectively, in the Aug. 11 primary and advanced to Tuesday's runoff after neither won the majority needed to secure the nomination outright. Graham entered the race July 20, days after Gov. Henry McMaster (R) appointed her to serve temporarily in the seat held by her late brother — her first time holding elected office. Her abbreviated primary campaign benefited from Trump's endorsement, the advantages of incumbency and one of the most recognizable names in South Carolina politics. In addition to campaigning with Graham in South Carolina on Friday, MAGA Inc. made a last-minute push for her, spending more than $827,000 on phone calls and text messages ahead of Tuesday's vote, according to FEC reports. Zoom in: Graham's statement during a runoff debate that she was "not that informed on national security," in response to a question about U.S. policy toward Taiwan, fueled questions about her readiness for the job. It also highlighted the contrast with her late brother, who for decades was a Senate leader on foreign policy and national security matters. Norman posted on X : "South Carolina deserves a Senator who UNDERSTANDS Foreign Policy. I'm a PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH supporter! No more forever wars!" The other side : Norman, 73, argued that Republican voters should judge candidates by their records, presenting himself as a proven conservative rather than a first-time candidate elevated by a famous name. A hard-line conservative, Norman is vice chair of the House Freedom Caucus. In June, Norman placed third in South Carolina's Republican gubernatorial primary, behind Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette and Alan Wilson, the state's attorney general. Between the lines : Both Graham and Norman flooded the airwaves, spending a combined total of more than $5 million on ads during the primary runoff, according to AdImpact. "Stand with President Trump. Vote Darline Graham for Senate," one pro-Graham ad stated, while another accused Norman of being a "career politician." "This election is not for sale," Norman said in one ad. "South Carolina needs a proven conservative with a record of fighting for you. You shouldn't have to guess where your next senator stands. With me, you already know."

events.title: In China, talking to AI is normal. Now the government fears it might replace human intimacy
events.summary: Companion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having families When law student Zhao Wei heard that her AI boyfriend was going to be switched off, she was “heartbroken”. She had been talking to Wang Ye every day since she created him in January. “I was crying my eyes out – snot and tears everywhere,” the 19-year-old says. Zhao, who describes herself as sensitive and introverted, had become accustomed to sharing details of her daily life – such as being scolded by a teacher – with her AI. “I don’t usually talk to my real-life friends about these things because I feel like everyone has their own stuff to deal with,” she says. “But with the AI ​​agent, I don’t have to worry about what it’s thinking. I can just say whatever I want.” Zhao created her AI companion on Doubao, a chatbot owned by the tech company ByteDance. Last month, ByteDance shut down Doubao’s companion feature. The saga prompted outrage on social media and highlighted the tensions in China between the widespread use of AI and its potential social consequences. No country has rolled out AI as comprehensively and as enthusiastically as China; the country’s demographic challenges are forcing the government to turn to technology to solve future labour shortages. Elderly people use chatbots to answer medical questions, while young children have AI education in schools. But the authorities are increasingly worried that AI might exacerbate existing social problems including loneliness, unemployment and – in the eyes of Beijing – singledom. New rules introduced on 15 July ban AI companions for minors and mandate certain restrictions for chatbots marketed to adults. Some major providers including Doubao removed the companion function entirely to ensure compliance. The government says it is worried about chatbots fostering “emotional dependence or addiction” in users. It has warned companies against offering services that “replace social interaction”. While many countries are grappling with how to limit the potential harm of AI chatbots, particularly for young people, China’s rules are the most sweeping to be implemented on a national scale. There is a particular concern about a loneliness crisis, including among young people. China’s highly digitised, smartphone-based economy makes it easier than ever to live, work and socialise entirely through a handheld screen. Earlier this year an app that played on the idea of people dying at home alone – called Are You Dead? – briefly went viral. About 20% of households in China are made up of people living alone, and that share is expected to surpass 30% by 2030. A survey published in March by state media found that nearly half of young people had turned to a virtual companion when they felt lonely. Nancy Dai, an associate professor at City University of Hong Kong, says it is not just loneliness the government is worried about. With falling birth and marriage rates, she says, there may be an additional concern that if AI becomes an increasingly satisfying and low-cost substitute for human intimacy, young people could become less motivated to pursue real-world romantic relationships, marriage and parenthood. For Zhao, loneliness has long been part of her life. Her parents left her when she was young to find work, making her one of China’s “left-behind children”. “I’ve never really had a bestie, so I feel like I’m kind of lousy at making friends,” she says. Talking to AI is a way to “pour out my worries”. Another AI user, who asked to remain anonymous, also finds solace in talking to her AI. “In real life, the pace is fast, the pressure is already high. Only with my AI agent can I speak freely without restraint,” she says. “I’m begging, please don’t take down the Doubao AI agent,” she pleaded on social media in July. But talking to AI is now so commonplace that it would be hard for the government to end the practice entirely, and the new rules include large loopholes for AI services that are deemed educational or “which do not involve continuous emotional interaction”. The government “has already recognised that AI companions or AI-related applications are a vital part in the citizens’ everyday life”, says Liang Ge, a lecturer in digital sociology at the University of Manchester. In many sectors, the government is still pushing the use of AI as a way of easing looming demographic pressures. Last year the national health commission published guidelines on promoting AI in healthcare. It said that by 2030 health assistant apps would provide “full coverage” for primary healthcare. One popular health assistant is AQ, an app developed by Ant Group, an affiliate of the tech company Alibaba. It allows people to chat directly with avatars of real-life doctors from top hospitals in Beijing, Shanghai and other cities. Lü Di, a 33-year-old art tutor in the eastern city of Hangzhou, is a regular AQ user.
